“I must insist on a little more quiet!” Holmes said sternly. “You have already put the success of this entire undertaking at risk. Would you please sit on one of those boxes and refrain from interfering?”

The solemn Mr. Merryweather perched on a crate, looking deeply offended. Holmes dropped to his knees and, using the lantern and a magnifying glass, closely examined the gaps between the paving stones. A few seconds satisfied him. He jumped up again and put the lens in his pocket.

“We have at least an hour,” he said. “They can scarcely begin until our good pawnbroker is safely in bed. After that they will waste no time: the sooner they finish, the longer they will have to escape. Doctor, as you have doubtless guessed, we are beneath the City branch of one of London's principal banks. Mr. Merryweather chairs its board of directors. He will explain why London's more audacious criminals should be particularly interested in this cellar just now.”
“It is the French gold,” the director whispered. “We have received several warnings that someone might try to steal it.”
“What French gold?”

“Some months ago we needed to increase our resources and borrowed thirty thousand napoleons from the Bank of France. Word has got out that we never needed to unpack the money, and that it is still here in the cellar. This crate I am sitting on holds two thousand napoleons, packed between sheets of lead foil. Our bullion reserve is much greater than a single branch normally keeps, and the directors have been uneasy about it.”

“With very good reason,” Holmes observed. “Now we must settle our arrangements. I expect events to reach their climax within the hour. For the moment, Mr. Merryweather, we need to cover the opening of that dark lantern.”
“And wait here in darkness?”

“I am afraid so. I brought a pack of cards, thinking that as a _partie carrée_—a group of four—we might let you have your rubber after all. But the enemy's preparations are too far advanced for us to risk a light. First we must take our positions. These men are bold. Even though we shall catch them off guard, they could hurt us if we are careless. I will stay behind this crate; you hide behind those. When I shine the light on them, move in quickly. Watson, if they fire, do not hesitate to shoot them down.”

Crouching behind a wooden case, I laid my cocked revolver on its top. Holmes slid the shutter over his lantern and plunged us into a darkness more complete than any I had known. The smell of heated metal reassured us that the flame was still there, ready to shine out instantly. With my nerves strung tight in anticipation, I found something dispiriting and oppressive in the sudden blackness and the vault's cold, damp air.
“There is only one way for them to retreat,” Holmes whispered. “Back through the house into Saxe-Coburg Square. Jones, I trust you made the arrangements I requested?”
“An inspector and two officers are waiting at the front door.”
“Then every exit is covered. Now we must wait without a sound.”

How long it seemed! Comparing our impressions afterwards, we discovered that only an hour and a quarter had passed. To me it felt as though the night must be nearly over, with dawn breaking overhead. My limbs ached and stiffened because I dared not shift position. My nerves, however, remained stretched to their utmost, and my hearing grew so sharp that I could hear each companion breathing softly. I could even distinguish the stout Jones's heavier, deeper intake of breath from the bank director's thin, sighing one. From where I crouched, I could see over the case towards the floor. Suddenly a gleam of light caught my eye.

At first it was merely a fierce little spark on the stone floor. It lengthened into a yellow line. Then, silently and without warning, a slit seemed to open, and a hand appeared—a white, almost feminine hand—feeling around in the middle of the small patch of light. For a minute or more it projected through the floor, its fingers moving restlessly. Then it vanished as suddenly as it had arrived. Darkness returned, except for the single glowing spark at a crack between the stones.

The darkness lasted only a moment. With a tearing, wrenching noise, a broad white stone tipped onto its side, exposing a square hole filled with lantern-light. A finely shaped, boyish face appeared above the edge and looked keenly around. Placing a hand on either side of the opening, the man lifted himself until his shoulders, then his waist, emerged and one knee rested on the rim. A moment later he stood beside the hole, pulling up a companion as small and supple as himself, with a pale face and a shock of intensely red hair.
“The way's clear,” he whispered. “Have you got the chisel and the bags? Great Scott! Jump, Archie, jump! I'll hang for this!”

Holmes had leaped forward and caught the intruder's collar. His companion dived into the hole. I heard cloth ripping as Jones grabbed at his coat-tails. A revolver barrel flashed in the light, but Holmes brought his hunting crop down on the man's wrist, and the pistol fell with a clink onto the stones.
“No use, John Clay,” Holmes said calmly. “You have no chance whatever.”
“I can see that,” the man replied with perfect composure. “Still, I think my friend has got away, though you seem to have kept his coat-tails.”
“Three men are waiting at the door to receive him,” Holmes said.
“Indeed! You appear to have arranged the whole affair most thoroughly. I must offer my compliments.”
“And mine to you,” Holmes replied. “The red-headed scheme was both original and effective.”
“You'll be seeing your friend shortly,” Jones said. “He goes down holes faster than I can. Hold out your hands while I put the cuffs on.”

“Kindly keep your dirty hands off me,” our prisoner said as the handcuffs rattled around his wrists. “Perhaps you do not realise that royal blood runs in my veins. And whenever you speak to me, have the courtesy to use ‘sir’ and ‘please’.”
“All right,” Jones replied, staring and sniggering. “Then would you please, sir, walk upstairs, so that we can find a cab to take your Highness to the police station?”
“Much better,” John Clay said serenely. With a sweeping bow to the three of us, he went off quietly in the detective's custody.

“Really, Mr. Holmes,” Merryweather said as we followed them out of the cellar, “I cannot imagine how the bank can properly thank or repay you. You have unquestionably uncovered and utterly defeated one of the most determined attempts at bank robbery I have ever encountered.”

“I had one or two private scores to settle with Mr. John Clay,” Holmes replied. “This affair has involved a little expense, which I shall expect the bank to reimburse. Beyond that, I am more than repaid by an experience that is exceptional in several ways, and by hearing the extraordinary history of the Red-headed League.”

“You see, Watson,” he explained in the early morning as we sat in Baker Street over whisky and soda, “the purpose was obvious from the start. That fantastic affair of the League's advertisement and the copying of the _Encyclopædia_ could have only one object: to get a rather dim pawnbroker out of the way for several hours each day. It was an odd method, but a better one would be difficult to devise. No doubt the colour of his accomplice's hair put the idea into Clay's ingenious mind. Four pounds a week was a temptation the man could hardly resist—and what did that amount to for men after thousands? They placed the advertisement. One scoundrel occupied a temporary office, the other urged the pawnbroker to apply, and between them they arranged to have him away every morning of the week. The moment I heard that the assistant had accepted half wages, I knew he must have a powerful reason for wanting that post.”
“But how did you work out what his reason could be?”

“If there had been women in the household, I would have suspected some sordid love affair. That, however, was ruled out. His business was small, and nothing in the house could justify such elaborate preparations and such expense. The object must therefore lie outside the house. What could it be? I remembered the assistant's interest in photography and his habit of disappearing into the cellar. The cellar! That gave me the loose end of this tangled clue. I then asked about the mysterious assistant and learned that I was dealing with one of London's calmest, boldest criminals. He was occupied in that cellar for hours every day, month after month. Once again, what could he be doing? I could think of only one answer: digging a tunnel to another building.

“That was as far as I had reasoned when we went to inspect the scene. You were surprised when I struck the pavement with my stick. I wanted to establish whether the cellar extended to the front or the rear. It did not extend forward. I then rang the bell and, as I hoped, the assistant answered. We had crossed swords before, but had never actually seen one another. I scarcely looked at his face: I wanted to examine his knees. You must have noticed how worn, creased, and stained the trousers were there. They told the story of hours spent digging. All that remained was to discover what he was digging towards. I walked around the corner, saw that the City and Suburban Bank backed onto our friend's property, and felt I had solved the problem. After the concert, while you were driving home, I visited Scotland Yard and the chairman of the bank's directors. You have seen the result.”
“How could you know they would attempt it tonight?” I asked.

“Well, closing the League's office showed that Mr. Wilson's presence no longer mattered to them. In other words, the tunnel was finished. They had to use it quickly, before it was discovered or the bullion was moved elsewhere. Saturday suited them better than any other day, giving them two days to escape. Taken together, all those reasons led me to expect them tonight.”
“You reasoned it through magnificently,” I exclaimed with sincere admiration. “Such a long chain of reasoning, yet every link is sound.”

“It kept boredom away,” he answered with a yawn. “Alas, I can already feel it returning. My whole life is a prolonged effort to escape the ordinary routine of existence. These small problems give me a means of doing so.”
“And meanwhile you do a service to humanity,” I added.
He gave a shrug. “Well, perhaps it does serve some little purpose after all,” he said. “‘_L’homme c’est rien—l’œuvre c’est tout_,’ as Gustave Flaubert wrote to George Sand.”

chapters.title: A Case of Identity
paragraphs: “My dear fellow,” Holmes said as we sat across the fire from one another in his Baker Street rooms, “life is infinitely stranger than anything a human mind could invent. We would never dare imagine things that are actually everyday occurrences. Suppose we could fly out of that window hand in hand, float above this great city, quietly lift its roofs, and look inside. Think of the odd happenings, the strange coincidences, the schemes and misunderstandings, the astonishing sequences of events stretching across generations and producing the most _outré_ outcomes. Beside that, all fiction, with its conventions and predictable endings, would seem utterly stale and unrewarding.”

“I am still not persuaded,” I replied. “The cases reported in the newspapers are usually plain and sordid enough. Our police reports take realism to its furthest extreme, yet we must admit that the result is neither captivating nor artistic.”

“Creating an impression of reality requires some judgement and selection,” Holmes observed. “Police reports lack that. They may devote more attention to a magistrate's platitudes than to the details that, for an observer, contain the whole affair's essential meaning. Believe me, nothing is so unnatural as the commonplace.”

I shook my head with a smile. “I can understand why you think so,” I said. “As unofficial adviser and helper to everyone on three continents who finds himself completely bewildered, you naturally encounter everything odd and extraordinary. But here”—I lifted the morning newspaper from the floor—“let us try a practical test. The first headline I see is ‘A husband's cruelty to his wife.’ There is half a column about it, but without reading a word I know it will be thoroughly familiar. Naturally there will be another woman, drink, a shove, a blow, a bruise, and a sympathetic sister or landlady. The crudest writer could imagine nothing cruder.”

“Unfortunately, that example rather undermines your argument,” Holmes replied, taking the paper and scanning it. “This is the Dundas separation case. As it happens, I was asked to clarify a few minor points. The husband never drank, there was no other woman, and his wife's complaint was that he had taken to finishing every meal by removing his false teeth and throwing them at her. You must admit that the average storyteller would be unlikely to think of that. Have a pinch of snuff, Doctor, and concede that your example has given me the victory.”

He offered me a snuffbox of old gold with a large amethyst set in the centre of its lid. Its magnificence contrasted so strongly with his unpretentious habits and simple way of life that I could not help remarking on it.
“Ah,” he said, “I had forgotten we had not met for several weeks. It is a small memento from the King of Bohemia, in return for my help with the Irene Adler papers.”
“And your ring?” I asked, looking at the remarkable brilliant-cut diamond flashing on his finger.

“A gift from Holland's reigning family. But the business I handled for them was so delicate that I cannot reveal it even to you, kind though you have been in recording one or two of my little problems.”
“Do you have any cases at present?” I asked with interest.

“Ten or twelve, but none with anything interesting about them. They are important, you understand, without being interesting. In fact, I generally find that unimportant affairs offer the best opportunities for observation and for that swift analysis of cause and effect which makes an investigation enjoyable. Major crimes tend to be simpler: the greater the crime, the more obvious its motive usually is. Apart from one rather complicated affair referred to me from Marseilles, none of my current cases has any feature of interest. Still, something better may arrive within a very few minutes, for unless I am much mistaken, that is one of my clients.”

He had got up and was standing between the open blinds, looking into the drab London street below. Over his shoulder I saw a large woman waiting on the opposite pavement. A heavy fur boa encircled her neck, and a large curled red feather decorated her broad-brimmed hat, tilted jauntily over one ear in the Duchess of Devonshire manner. Beneath this elaborate array, she glanced nervously and uncertainly up at our windows, rocking back and forth and fiddling with the buttons of her gloves. Suddenly she plunged forward like a swimmer launching himself from the bank, hurried across the road, and gave the bell a sharp ring.

“I recognise those symptoms,” Holmes said, tossing his cigarette into the fire. “Rocking back and forth on the pavement always indicates an _affaire de cœur_. She wants advice but fears the matter may be too delicate to discuss. Even here, though, we can make distinctions. A woman seriously wronged by a man no longer hesitates on the pavement; a snapped bell-wire is the usual sign. We may therefore infer a love affair, but one that has left the young lady bewildered or distressed rather than angry. Here she comes to settle our doubts herself.”

As he finished, someone tapped at the door. The uniformed pageboy came in to announce Miss Mary Sutherland. Behind his small black-clad figure the lady loomed like a merchant ship under full sail following a tiny pilot boat. Holmes greeted her with his characteristic easy courtesy. He closed the door, bowed her into an armchair, and studied her in that peculiarly detached yet minute way of his.
“With your short sight,” he asked, “do you not find so much typewriting rather a strain?”

“At first I did,” she replied, “but now I know where all the letters are without looking.” Then the full meaning of his question struck her. She gave a violent start and looked up, fear and amazement on her broad, good-natured face. “You have heard about me, Mr. Holmes!” she cried. “How else could you know all that?”
“Never mind,” Holmes said, laughing. “Knowing things is my profession. Perhaps I have taught myself to notice what other people miss. Otherwise, why would you come to me for advice?”

“I came because Mrs. Etherege told me about you, sir. You found her husband so easily after the police and everybody else had given him up for dead. Oh, Mr. Holmes, I wish you could do as much for me. I'm not wealthy, but I have a hundred pounds a year of my own, besides what I earn at the typewriter. I would give every penny to discover what has happened to Mr. Hosmer Angel.”
“What made you leave home in such a hurry to consult me?” Holmes asked, pressing his fingertips together and looking at the ceiling.

Once again a startled expression crossed Miss Mary Sutherland's rather vacant face. “Yes, I did rush out of the house,” she said. “Mr. Windibank—that is, my father—was taking the whole affair so lightly that it made me angry. He wouldn't go to the police or to you. At last, when he still refused to do anything and kept saying no harm had been done, I lost my temper, put on my things, and came straight here.”
“Your father?” Holmes said. “Surely you mean your stepfather, since his surname is different.”
“Yes, my stepfather. I call him father, though it does sound odd, considering he is only five years and two months older than I am.”
“And is your mother still living?”

“Oh yes, Mother is alive and well. I wasn't at all pleased, Mr. Holmes, when she married again so soon after Father's death—and to a man nearly fifteen years younger than herself. Father was a plumber in the Tottenham Court Road. He left a good business, which Mother carried on with Mr. Hardy, the foreman. But when Mr. Windibank arrived, he made her sell it. He thought himself much above that sort of thing, being a travelling salesman for a wine firm. They received £ 4700 for the goodwill and their interest in the business, far less than Father could have obtained if he had lived.”
I had expected Holmes to grow impatient with this rambling, apparently irrelevant account. Instead, he listened with the closest possible attention.
“Your own small income,” he asked, “does that come from the business?”

“Oh no, sir. It is entirely separate. My uncle Ned in Auckland left it to me. The money is in New Zealand stock at four and a half per cent: two thousand five hundred pounds altogether. But I can only use the interest.”

“This is extremely interesting,” Holmes said. “With as much as a hundred a year, besides your earnings, no doubt you travel a little and allow yourself plenty of pleasures. I believe an unmarried lady can live very comfortably on about sixty pounds.”

“I could manage on much less, Mr. Holmes. But while I live at home, I don't want to be a burden, so they have the use of my income for as long as I stay with them. Of course, it is only for that period. Mr. Windibank collects the interest every quarter and gives it to Mother. I find I can manage quite well on my typewriting earnings. I get twopence a sheet and can often finish fifteen to twenty sheets a day.”

“You have explained your circumstances very clearly,” said Holmes. “This is my friend, Dr. Watson. You may speak as freely in front of him as you would to me alone. Now please tell us everything about your relationship with Mr. Hosmer Angel.”

Miss Sutherland blushed and nervously picked at her jacket's fringe. “I first met him at the gasfitters' ball,” she said. “They used to send Father tickets when he was alive. Afterwards they remembered us and sent them to Mother. Mr. Windibank didn't want us to attend. He never wanted us to go anywhere. Even if I wanted to join a Sunday-school outing, he would become furious. But this time I was determined to go, and go I would. What right had he to stop me? He said the company wasn't suitable for us, though all Father's friends would be there. Then he said I had nothing to wear, when I had my purple plush dress that had never even left its drawer. Finally, when nothing else worked, he went to France on business for his firm. Mother and I went to the ball with Mr. Hardy, our former foreman. That was where I met Mr. Hosmer Angel.”
“I suppose Mr. Windibank was very angry when he returned from France and learned you had attended the ball,” Holmes said.
“Actually, he took it very well. I remember him laughing and shrugging, saying there was no point refusing a woman anything because she would get her own way.”
“I understand. So you met a gentleman called Mr. Hosmer Angel at the gasfitters' ball.”

“Yes, sir. We met that evening. The next day he called to ask whether we had reached home safely. After that we met him—or rather, Mr. Holmes, I met him twice for walks. But then Father came home again, and Mr. Hosmer Angel could no longer visit.”
“He couldn't?”

“Well, Father disliked anything of that kind. He would have kept all visitors away if he could. He always said a woman should find happiness within her family circle. But as I told Mother, a woman needs a family circle of her own first, and I hadn't got mine yet.”
“What about Mr. Hosmer Angel? Did he do nothing to try to see you?”

“Father was due to return to France in a week. Hosmer wrote that we had better wait until he left before seeing each other: it would be safer. Meanwhile we could correspond, and he wrote every day. I brought in the morning letters, so Father needn't know.”
“Had you become engaged to him by then?”
“Oh yes, Mr. Holmes. We got engaged after our very first walk. Hosmer—Mr. Angel—worked as a cashier in an office on Leadenhall Street, and—”
“Which office was it?”
“That's the dreadful part, Mr. Holmes: I don't know.”
“Where was he living, then?”
“He slept at the office.”
“But you do not know the address?”
“No—only that it was in Leadenhall Street.”
“Then where did you send your letters?”

“To the Leadenhall Street Post Office, for him to collect. He said the other clerks would tease him about receiving letters from a lady if they came to his office. I offered to type mine, as he typed his, but he wouldn't agree. He said my handwritten letters felt as though they came directly from me, whereas with typed letters he would always feel the machine had come between us. That shows how much he loved me, Mr. Holmes, and the little things he thought about.”
“Very revealing,” said Holmes. “I have long made it a principle that little things are by far the most important. Can you recall any other small details about Mr. Hosmer Angel?”

“He was terribly shy, Mr. Holmes. He preferred walking with me in the evening, rather than by daylight, because he disliked attracting attention. He was very quiet and gentlemanly. Even his voice was gentle. He told me that quinsy and swollen glands when he was young had weakened his throat, leaving him with a hesitant way of speaking in whispers. His clothes were always good, very neat and plain. But his eyes were weak, like mine, and he wore tinted spectacles to protect them from the glare.”
“And what happened when your stepfather, Mr. Windibank, went back to France?”

“Mr. Hosmer Angel began calling again and suggested we should get married before Father returned. He was desperately serious. He made me put my hands on the Testament and swear that, whatever happened, I would remain faithful. Mother said he was quite right to ask for the oath, and it proved how deeply he loved me. She supported him from the start and was even fonder of him than I was. When they began talking about a wedding within the week, I asked about Father. Both of them said not to worry about him, but simply to tell him afterwards; Mother promised to settle it with him. I wasn't comfortable with that, Mr. Holmes. It seemed odd to ask his permission when he was only a few years older than me, but I didn't want anything done secretly. So I wrote to Father in Bordeaux, where his firm's French offices are. The letter came back on the very morning of the wedding.”
“So it failed to reach him?”
“Yes, sir. He had left for England just before it arrived.”
“Ah! How unfortunate. So the wedding was set for Friday. Were you to marry in a church?”

“Yes, sir, very quietly, at St. Saviour's near King's Cross. Afterwards we planned to have breakfast at the St. Pancras Hotel. Hosmer fetched us in a hansom. As there were two of us, he put us both into it and took a four-wheeler himself, the only other cab in the street. We reached the church first. When his cab arrived, we waited for him to get out, but he didn't. The driver climbed down from his seat and looked inside. Nobody was there! He said he couldn't imagine what had become of the gentleman, whom he had seen get in with his own eyes. That was last Friday, Mr. Holmes. Since then I have neither seen nor heard anything that could explain what happened to him.”
“It appears to me that someone has treated you very shamefully,” Holmes said.

“Oh no, sir! He was far too good and kind to abandon me like that. All morning he kept telling me to be faithful whatever happened. Even if something entirely unexpected separated us, I must remember my promise to him, and that sooner or later he would hold me to it. It was strange talk for the morning of a wedding, but what has happened since makes sense of it.”
“It most certainly does. Your own belief, then, is that some unexpected disaster has overtaken him?”
“Yes, sir. I think he knew there might be danger; otherwise he wouldn't have spoken like that. And I believe whatever he feared did happen.”
“But you have no idea what that danger might have been?”
“None.”
“One more thing: how did your mother respond?”
“She became angry and told me never to mention the matter again.”
“And your father—did you tell him about it?”

“Yes. He seemed to agree that something must have happened, and that I would hear from Hosmer again. As he said, why would anybody take me right to the church door and then abandon me? If Hosmer had borrowed money, or married me and had my money settled on him, there might be a reason. But he was very independent about money and wouldn't so much as look at a shilling of mine. Yet what can have happened? Why can't he write? Thinking about it nearly drives me mad, and I cannot sleep a wink.” She took a small handkerchief from her muff and began sobbing heavily into it.

“I will look into it for you,” Holmes said, getting up, “and I am confident we shall reach a definite conclusion. Leave the burden with me now, and try not to dwell on it any longer. Above all, try to let Mr. Hosmer Angel disappear from your thoughts as he has disappeared from your life.”
“Then you don't believe I shall see him again?”
“I am afraid not.”
“But what has become of him?”
“Leave that question to me. I would like a precise description of him, and any of his letters you can let me have.”
“I placed a notice about him in last Saturday's _Chronicle_,” she replied. “Here is the cutting, and here are four of his letters.”
“Thank you. What is your address?”
“No. 31 Lyon Place, Camberwell.”
“You never knew Mr. Angel's address, I understand. Where does your father work?”
“He travels for Westhouse & Marbank, the large claret-importing firm on Fenchurch Street.”

“Thank you. You have explained everything very clearly. Leave these papers with me and remember my advice. Treat this entire affair as a closed book, and do not let it influence the rest of your life.”
“You are very kind, Mr. Holmes, but I cannot. I will remain faithful to Hosmer. When he comes back, he will find me waiting.”

Despite her absurd hat and vacant expression, something in our visitor's simple trust was noble enough to command respect. She placed her small packet of papers on the table and left, promising to return whenever we sent for her.

For several minutes Holmes said nothing. His fingertips remained together, his legs stretched out before him, his eyes fixed on the ceiling. Then he took his old, oily clay pipe from the rack—that pipe which served him like an adviser—and lit it. He leaned back in his chair, thick blue coils of smoke rising around him, his face expressing utter languor.

“An interesting subject for study, that young woman,” he remarked. “More interesting than her little difficulty, which is rather familiar. My index will show you comparable cases at Andover in '77, and something similar at The Hague last year. Still, old as the idea is, one or two details were new to me. The young lady herself, however, offered a great deal to learn from.”
“You seemed to read a great deal about her that I could not see at all,” I remarked.

“You could see it, Watson; you simply failed to notice it. You missed everything significant because you did not know where to look. I cannot make you appreciate the importance of sleeves, the information a thumbnail offers, or the momentous conclusions that may depend on a bootlace. Tell me what you learned from her appearance. Describe it.”

“Well, her straw hat was slate-coloured, with a broad brim and a brick-red feather. She wore a black jacket decorated with black beads and a fringe of little jet ornaments. Her dress was brown, a shade darker than coffee, with purple plush at the neck and sleeves. Her greyish gloves had a hole at the right forefinger. I did not notice her boots. She wore small, round gold earrings that hung down, and generally looked fairly prosperous in a comfortable, easy-going, rather vulgar way.”
Holmes gave a quiet chuckle and gently clapped his hands together.

“Upon my word, Watson, you are making splendid progress. You have done very well indeed. You missed every important point, admittedly, but you have grasped the method, and your eye for colour is sharp. Never rely on an overall impression, my boy: attend to the details. With a woman I look first at her sleeve; with a man, the knee of his trousers is perhaps the better starting point. As you noticed, her sleeves were trimmed with plush, an excellent material for preserving marks. The double line just above the wrist, where a typist rests against the table, showed beautifully. A hand-operated sewing machine produces a similar mark, but only on the left arm, on the side away from the thumb. It does not cross the widest part of the arm as this one did. Then I looked at her face. Seeing the marks of a pince-nez on both sides of her nose, I ventured a comment about short sight and typewriting, which appeared to startle her.”
“It certainly startled me.”

“But surely it was plain enough. Looking down, I then noticed something surprisingly interesting: her boots looked similar, but did not form a pair. One toe-cap had a little decoration; the other was plain. On one boot, only the bottom two of five buttons were fastened; on the other, the first, third, and fifth. If a young lady otherwise neatly dressed leaves home wearing mismatched boots only partly buttoned, concluding that she left in a hurry requires no great effort.”
“What else did you see?” I asked, fascinated as always by my friend's penetrating reasoning.

“In passing I noticed that she had written a note after dressing but before leaving the house. You saw the tear at the right glove's forefinger, but apparently missed the violet ink on both the glove and the finger. She had written hurriedly, dipping her pen too far into the ink. It must have been this morning; otherwise the stain on her finger would no longer be so distinct. Entertaining, though elementary. But I must return to work, Watson. Would you read out the description of Mr. Hosmer Angel in the advertisement?”

I raised the printed cutting towards the light. It read: “Missing on the morning of the fourteenth, a gentleman named Hosmer Angel. About five feet seven inches tall; solid build; sallow skin; black hair, with a small bald patch in the centre; thick black side-whiskers and moustache; tinted spectacles; a slight speech impairment. Last seen wearing a black frock-coat with silk facings, black waistcoat, gold Albert chain, grey Harris tweed trousers, and brown gaiters over elastic-sided boots. Known to have worked in an office on Leadenhall Street. Anyone bringing”—and so on, and so on.

“That is enough,” Holmes said. Looking over the letters, he continued, “These are quite ordinary. They offer no clue to Mr. Angel beyond a single quotation from Balzac. There is, however, one remarkable feature which will surely catch your attention.”
“They were typed,” I observed.

“More than that: the signature was typed as well. See the neat little ‘Hosmer Angel’ at the foot of the page. There is a date, but no address at the top beyond the rather vague ‘Leadenhall Street’. That signature is highly suggestive—indeed, we may call it conclusive.”
“Conclusive of what?”
“My dear fellow, can you really fail to see how directly it concerns the case?”
“I cannot say I see it—unless he wanted to deny the signature if she sued him for breaking his promise to marry.”

“No, that is not it. Still, two letters should settle everything. I shall send one to a firm in the City and the other to her stepfather, Mr. Windibank, asking him to meet us here tomorrow evening at six. It is as well to conduct our business with the male relatives. Until replies arrive, Doctor, there is nothing more to do. We can put this little problem aside for the time being.”

I had seen so many proofs of my friend's subtle reasoning and extraordinary energy in action that I felt sure his calm confidence rested on solid grounds. He could not be treating this strange mystery so easily without good reason. I had known him fail only once, over the King of Bohemia and Irene Adler's photograph. When I remembered the uncanny affair of the Sign of Four and the extraordinary events of the Study in Scarlet, I felt that a puzzle would have to be very tangled indeed to defeat him.

I left him then, still puffing away at his black clay pipe, convinced that when I returned the following evening I would find him in possession of all the clues needed to establish the identity of Miss Mary Sutherland's disappearing bridegroom.

A seriously ill patient was occupying my own attention at the time, and I spent the entire following day at the sufferer's bedside. I was not free until nearly six, when I jumped into a hansom and drove to Baker Street, rather afraid of arriving too late to witness the little mystery's _dénouement_. But Holmes was alone, half asleep, his long, thin body curled into the depths of his armchair. A formidable collection of bottles and test-tubes, together with the sharp, clean smell of hydrochloric acid, showed that he had spent the day on his beloved chemical experiments.
“Well, have you found the answer?” I asked on entering.
“Yes. It proved to be bisulphate of baryta.”
“No, no—the mystery!” I exclaimed.

“Oh, that! I was thinking of the salt I have been examining. There was never any mystery about this affair, although, as I said yesterday, some details are interesting. The only difficulty is that I fear no law can reach the scoundrel responsible.”
“Then who was he, and why did he abandon Miss Sutherland?”
I had scarcely finished speaking, and Holmes had not yet opened his mouth to answer, when we heard a heavy footstep in the passage and a knock at the door.
“That will be the young lady's stepfather, Mr. James Windibank,” Holmes said. “He wrote to say he would arrive at six. Come in!”

The newcomer was a stocky man of medium height, about thirty, clean-shaven and sallow, with a smooth, ingratiating manner. His grey eyes were extraordinarily sharp and penetrating. He looked enquiringly from one of us to the other, placed his glossy top-hat on the sideboard, and, with a small bow, edged into the nearest chair.
“Good evening, Mr. James Windibank,” Holmes said. “I believe you sent this typed letter arranging to see me at six?”

“Yes, sir. I am afraid I am slightly late, but my time is not entirely my own. I regret that Miss Sutherland has troubled you with this little business. Such dirty linen is much better kept out of public view. I strongly opposed her coming, but, as you may have noticed, she is excitable and impulsive, and difficult to manage once she has made up her mind. Naturally, I objected less to you, since you have no official connection with the police. Still, nobody wants a family misfortune of this kind broadcast abroad. Besides, it is money wasted. How could you possibly find this Hosmer Angel?”
“On the contrary,” Holmes replied quietly, “I have every reason to expect that I shall succeed in finding Mr. Hosmer Angel.”
Windibank gave a violent start and let his gloves fall. “I am delighted to hear that,” he said.

“It is curious,” Holmes observed, “how individual a typewriter can be—quite as distinctive as someone's handwriting. Unless they are brand new, no two machines produce exactly the same result. Some letters wear more than others, and some wear on one side only. In this note of yours, Mr. Windibank, you will notice that the ‘e’ is slightly blurred throughout, while the tail of the ‘r’ has a small defect. There are fourteen further characteristics, but those are the easiest to see.”
“That machine handles all our office correspondence, so it is probably rather worn,” our visitor replied, watching Holmes closely with his bright little eyes.

“Now let me show you something genuinely interesting, Mr. Windibank,” Holmes continued. “One of these days I mean to write another short monograph, this time on the typewriter's connection with crime. I have given the subject some attention. Here are four letters supposedly written by the missing gentleman. Every one is typed. In each, you find not only blurred ‘e’s and ‘r’s without tails, but also, if you care to examine them through my magnifying glass, all fourteen of the other characteristics I mentioned.”
Windibank sprang up and seized his hat. “I cannot waste my time on this fanciful nonsense, Mr. Holmes. If you can catch the man, do so, and let me know when you have.”
“Certainly,” Holmes replied, walking to the door and locking it. “Then let me inform you that I have caught him!”
“What! Where?” Mr. Windibank shouted, turning white to the lips and looking around him like a rat caught in a trap.

“Oh, that will not do—not at all,” Holmes said smoothly. “There is no escape from this, Mr. Windibank. It is entirely transparent. You paid me a poor compliment in suggesting that I could not solve such a simple problem. There! Sit down, and we can discuss it.”
Our visitor sank into a chair, his face deathly pale, sweat gleaming on his forehead. “It—it isn't grounds for legal action,” he stammered.

“I very much fear you are right. But between ourselves, Windibank, in its petty way this is as cruel, selfish, and heartless a trick as I have ever encountered. Let me go through what happened, and correct me wherever I am wrong.”

The man huddled in his chair, his head bowed to his chest, looking utterly defeated. Holmes rested his feet on a corner of the mantelpiece and leaned back, hands in pockets. He began to speak, seemingly more to himself than to us.

“A man married a much older woman for her money,” he began. “While her daughter lived with them, he also enjoyed the daughter's income. For people in their circumstances it was a substantial sum; losing it would make a serious difference. Keeping it was worth some effort. The daughter was good-natured and agreeable, but also loving and warm-hearted. With her decent looks and small income, she plainly would not remain unmarried for long. Her marriage would mean losing a hundred pounds a year. How, then, could her stepfather prevent it? First he did the obvious: kept her at home and forbade her to mix with people her own age. Soon, though, he saw that this would not work indefinitely. She became restless, asserted her rights, and finally declared that she would attend a particular ball. What did her clever stepfather do next? He devised a plan that spoke better for his ingenuity than for his heart. With his wife's knowledge and assistance, he disguised himself: tinted spectacles hid those sharp eyes, a moustache and thick side-whiskers concealed his face, and that clear voice became a persuasive whisper. Her short sight made him doubly safe. He appeared as Mr. Hosmer Angel and excluded rival suitors by courting her himself.”
“It began as a joke,” our visitor groaned. “We never imagined she would take it so much to heart.”

“Very possibly not. Whatever your intention, she certainly did take it to heart. Convinced that her stepfather was in France, she never for a moment suspected any deception. His attentions flattered her, and her mother's loudly expressed approval strengthened their effect. Then Mr. Angel began visiting the house: clearly the affair had to be carried as far as possible to make it effective. Meetings followed, then an engagement, which would prevent her affections from wandering towards anyone else. But the deception could not last forever. Pretending to travel to France was becoming awkward. The obvious solution was to end the affair so dramatically that it left a lasting mark on her mind and kept her from considering another suitor for a long time. Hence the vows of loyalty sworn on a Testament; hence the hints that something might happen on the very morning of the wedding. James Windibank wanted Miss Sutherland so devoted to Hosmer Angel, and so uncertain of his fate, that she would refuse to listen to another man for at least ten years. He brought her to the church door. Unable to go any further, he conveniently disappeared, using the old trick of entering one door of a four-wheeler and leaving through the other. That, I believe, is the sequence of events, Mr. Windibank!”
During Holmes's account our visitor had regained some of his confidence. He now stood, a cold sneer spreading across his pale face.

“Perhaps so, Mr. Holmes, perhaps not,” he said. “But if you are as clever as you think, you should know that you are the one breaking the law now. Nothing I have done from the outset gives grounds for action. Keeping that door locked, however, makes you liable for assault and unlawful restraint.”

“As you say, the law cannot touch you,” Holmes replied, unlocking the door and flinging it open. “Yet no man ever deserved punishment more. If the young lady has a brother or a friend, he ought to take a whip to your shoulders. By Jove!” he continued, reddening at the man's malicious sneer. “This is no part of my duty to my client, but there is a hunting crop within reach, and I think I shall allow myself the pleasure of—” He took two quick strides towards it. Before he could grasp it, however, footsteps clattered wildly down the stairs and the heavy front door slammed. From the window we could see Mr. James Windibank racing down the street.

“What a cold-blooded villain!” Holmes said with a laugh, dropping back into his chair. “He will go from one crime to another until he does something dreadful and finishes on the gallows. In some respects, the case has not been altogether uninteresting.”
“Even now, I cannot follow every step in your reasoning,” I remarked.

“From the beginning, of course, it was plain that Mr. Hosmer Angel must have had a powerful reason for behaving so strangely. It was equally clear that the stepfather was the only man who, as far as we could see, actually benefited from this affair. The fact that they never appeared together was suggestive: one always came on the scene when the other was away. The tinted spectacles and peculiar voice hinted at a disguise, as did the thick whiskers. His curious decision to type his signature confirmed all my suspicions. That implied his handwriting was so familiar to her that she would recognise even the tiniest specimen. You see, these separate facts, together with many smaller ones, all pointed in the same direction.”
“How did you confirm those suspicions?”

“Once I had identified my man, confirmation was easy. I knew which firm employed him. I took the printed description and removed everything a disguise could produce—the whiskers, spectacles, and voice. Then I sent it to the firm, asking whether it described any of their travelling salesmen. I had already noted the typewriter's peculiarities, so I wrote to Windibank at his business address and invited him here. As I expected, he typed his reply, reproducing the same small but distinctive defects. The same post brought a letter from Westhouse & Marbank of Fenchurch Street confirming that the description matched their employee James Windibank in every detail. _Voilà tout_!”
“And what of Miss Sutherland?”

“She would not believe me if I told her. Perhaps you remember the old Persian saying: ‘There is danger for him who taketh the tiger cub, and danger also for whoso snatches a delusion from a woman.’ Hafiz contains as much wisdom as Horace, and as much understanding of the world.”

chapters.title: The Boscombe Valley Mystery
paragraphs: One morning my wife and I were having breakfast when the maid brought a telegram. It was from Sherlock Holmes, and read as follows:

“Can you spare a couple of days? Just summoned by telegram from west of England concerning Boscombe Valley tragedy. Would be glad of your company. Excellent air and scenery. Taking 11:15 from Paddington.”
“What do you think, dear?” my wife asked across the table. “Shall you go?”
“I don't quite know. I have rather a long list of patients just now.”
“Anstruther could attend to them for you. You have looked a little pale recently, and I think a change would help. Besides, Mr. Holmes's cases always interest you so much.”
“It would be ungrateful if they didn't, considering what one of them brought me,” I replied. “But if I am going, I must pack immediately. There is only half an hour.”

Camp life in Afghanistan had at least taught me to be ready to travel at short notice. My needs were simple and few. In less than half an hour I was in a cab with my travelling bag, rattling towards Paddington. Holmes was walking up and down the platform. His long grey travelling-cloak and close-fitting cloth cap made his tall, spare figure look taller and thinner still.

“It is extremely kind of you to come, Watson,” he said. “Having someone beside me whom I can trust completely makes a great difference. Local assistance is invariably either useless or prejudiced. Reserve those two corner seats, if you will, while I buy our tickets.”

We had the compartment to ourselves, apart from the enormous collection of newspapers Holmes had brought. He searched through them and read, pausing to make notes or reflect, until we passed Reading. Then he suddenly crumpled the whole lot into an immense ball and threw it onto the luggage rack.
“Have you heard anything about this case?” he asked.
“Nothing whatever. I haven't read a newspaper for several days.”

“The London papers have carried rather incomplete reports. I have been reading all the recent issues to get the details straight. From what I can gather, it seems to be one of those simple cases that are exceptionally difficult.”
“That sounds rather contradictory.”

“Yet it is profoundly true. An unusual feature almost always supplies a clue. The more ordinary and undistinguished a crime, the harder it is to fix responsibility for it. Here, however, they have built a very serious case against the murdered man's son.”
“So there has been a murder?”

“That is what is supposed to have happened. I shall take nothing for granted until I have had a chance to investigate personally. Let me briefly explain the situation as far as I have been able to understand it.

“Boscombe Valley is a rural district near Ross in Herefordshire. The principal landowner is Mr. John Turner, who made his fortune in Australia and came back to England some years ago. He let one of his farms, Hatherley, to Mr. Charles McCarthy, who had also lived in Australia. They knew each other in the colonies, so it was natural that, when settling down, they chose to live close together. Turner was apparently the wealthier of the two, making McCarthy his tenant. Nevertheless, they seem to have remained on entirely equal terms and often spent time together. McCarthy had one son, aged eighteen; Turner had an only daughter of the same age. Both men were widowers. They appear to have avoided the neighbouring English families and lived quietly, although both McCarthys enjoyed sport and were often seen at local race meetings. McCarthy employed two servants, a man and a girl. Turner's household was larger—at least half a dozen. That is all I have learned about the families. Now for the events.

“On June 3rd, which was last Monday, McCarthy left his house at Hatherley at about three in the afternoon and walked to Boscombe Pool. It is a small lake formed where the stream running along the valley widens. That morning he had been to Ross with his manservant and had told the man to hurry because he had an important appointment to keep at three. He never returned from that appointment alive.

“The distance from Hatherley Farmhouse to Boscombe Pool is a quarter of a mile. Two people saw him cover that distance: an elderly woman whose name is not given, and William Crowder, a gamekeeper employed by Turner. Both state that McCarthy was alone. Crowder adds that a few minutes afterwards he saw the son, Mr. James McCarthy, heading the same way with a gun under his arm. He believes the father was still in sight and the son was following him. He gave it no further thought until that evening, when he learned of the tragedy that had taken place.

“Both McCarthys were seen again after William Crowder, the gamekeeper, had lost sight of them. Thick woods surround Boscombe Pool, with only a narrow strip of grass and reeds at the water's edge. Patience Moran, the fourteen-year-old daughter of the Boscombe Valley estate's lodge-keeper, was gathering flowers in one of those woods. In her statement she says she saw Mr. McCarthy and his son beside the lake, at the edge of the trees, apparently quarrelling violently. The elder McCarthy was using very strong language, and she saw the son raise a hand as though to hit him. Frightened by their violence, she ran home and told her mother she had left the McCarthys arguing near the pool and feared they were about to fight. Scarcely had she finished when young McCarthy ran up to the lodge, saying he had found his father dead in the wood and asking for the lodge-keeper's help. He was extremely agitated, without either hat or gun. Fresh blood was noticed on his right hand and sleeve. Following him, they found the body lying on the grass beside the pool. Repeated blows from a heavy, blunt weapon had crushed the head. The injuries could readily have been caused by the butt of the son's gun, which lay in the grass a few paces away. In these circumstances the young man was arrested immediately. Tuesday's inquest returned a verdict of wilful murder; on Wednesday he appeared before the Ross magistrates, who sent the case to the next Assizes. Those are the main facts presented to the coroner and the police court.”
“I can scarcely imagine stronger evidence against anyone,” I said. “If circumstantial evidence ever identified a criminal, surely it does here.”

“Circumstantial evidence is a very treacherous thing,” Holmes answered thoughtfully. “It can seem to point straight towards one conclusion. Shift your viewpoint slightly, however, and you may find it pointing just as firmly towards something completely different. Still, we must admit that the case against this young man looks extremely serious, and he may well be guilty. Several neighbours believe him innocent, however, including Miss Turner, the daughter of the adjoining landowner. They have engaged Lestrade—you will remember him from the Study in Scarlet—to investigate on his behalf. Lestrade was puzzled and passed the case to me. Hence two middle-aged gentlemen are rushing west at fifty miles an hour, instead of peacefully digesting breakfast at home.”
“I fear the facts are so clear,” I said, “that there will be little credit for you in solving this case.”

“Nothing is more misleading than an obvious fact,” he replied, laughing. “Besides, we might discover other obvious facts that Mr. Lestrade has entirely missed. You know me too well to think it mere boasting when I say I shall either establish or demolish his theory by methods he could neither use nor even understand. To take the nearest example: I can plainly see that your bedroom window is on your right. Yet I doubt whether Mr. Lestrade would notice even something as self-evident as that.”
“How on earth can you—”

“My dear fellow, I know you very well, and I know the military neatness that is characteristic of you. You shave every morning, and at this time of year you do so in sunlight. Yet on your left side the shave becomes less thorough towards the back, positively untidy around the angle of the jaw. Clearly that side receives less light. I cannot imagine a man with your habits inspecting himself in even light and accepting such a result. I mention this only as a small example of the use of observation and inference. It is my _métier_, and may possibly prove useful in the investigation ahead. The inquest brought out one or two further small points worth examining.”
“Which points are those?”

“Apparently the arrest did not occur on the spot, but only after they had returned to Hatherley Farm. When the police inspector informed him that he was under arrest, he replied that he was not surprised to hear it and deserved no better. That remark naturally removed any remaining trace of doubt from the minds of the jurors at the inquest.”
“That was a confession!” I exclaimed.
“No: he followed it with a declaration of innocence.”
“After such a damning sequence of events, it was at least an extremely suspicious thing to say.”

“Quite the reverse,” said Holmes. “It is the clearest break I can presently see in the clouds. Innocent or not, he could hardly be so stupid as to miss how badly the circumstances looked for him. If he had shown surprise at being arrested, or pretended indignation, I would have found that highly suspicious. Surprise and anger would be unnatural in those circumstances, although a calculating man might think them his best approach. His honest acceptance indicates either innocence or remarkable self-command and firmness. Nor was his remark about deserving it unnatural. He stood beside his father's dead body. That very day he had undoubtedly forgotten his duty as a son far enough to argue with him, and even, according to the little girl whose evidence matters so much, to raise his hand as though to strike him. The remorse and self-reproach expressed in his words seem to me signs of a sound mind rather than a guilty one.”
I shook my head. “Plenty of men have been hanged on much weaker evidence,” I said.
“Indeed they have. And plenty of men have been hanged unjustly.”
“What is the young man's own version of events?”
“I am afraid it is not very reassuring for his supporters, although one or two points in it do suggest possibilities. Here is the account; you can read it for yourself.”

From his bundle he selected a copy of the local Herefordshire newspaper. Folding back the sheet, he pointed to the paragraph in which the unfortunate young man had given his own account of what happened. I settled comfortably into my corner of the railway compartment and read it with great attention. The statement ran as follows:

“Mr. James McCarthy, the deceased's only son, was then called and gave the following evidence: ‘I had spent three days in Bristol and returned home only on Monday morning, the 3rd. My father was out when I arrived. The maid told me he had driven to Ross with the groom, John Cobb. Soon afterwards I heard his trap enter the yard. Looking through my window, I saw him get out and hurry away, though I did not know which direction he took. I then picked up my gun and strolled towards Boscombe Pool, intending to visit the rabbit warren on its far side. On the way I saw William Crowder, as he has testified, but he is wrong to think I was following my father. I had no idea Father was ahead. About a hundred yards from the pool, I heard “Cooee!”—a signal we commonly used to call one another. I hurried forward and found him beside the pool. He seemed very surprised to see me and asked rather roughly why I was there. Our conversation turned into an argument and nearly a fight, for Father had a violent temper. When I saw that he was losing control, I left him and turned back towards Hatherley. I had gone no more than 150 yards when a dreadful cry behind me made me run back. I found him dying on the ground, his head terribly wounded. Dropping my gun, I took him in my arms, but he died almost immediately. I knelt beside him for several minutes, then went for help to Mr. Turner's lodge-keeper, whose house was nearest. When I returned to Father, I saw nobody near him, and I do not know how he received his injuries. He was not popular, being cold and forbidding in manner, but to my knowledge he had no active enemies. I know nothing more about it.’
“The Coroner: Did your father say anything to you before his death?
“Witness: He muttered a few words. All I could make out was some reference to a rat.
“The Coroner: What did you take that to mean?
“Witness: It meant nothing to me. I assumed he was delirious.
“The Coroner: What subject caused this last argument between you and your father?
“Witness: I would rather not answer that.
“The Coroner: I am afraid I must insist on an answer.
“Witness: I really cannot tell you. I can assure you it has no connection with the tragic events that followed.
“The Coroner: The court must decide that. I scarcely need remind you that refusing to answer will seriously damage your position in any further proceedings.
“Witness: I must nevertheless refuse to answer.
“The Coroner: I understand you and your father regularly used the call ‘Cooee’ as a signal?
“Witness: We did.
“The Coroner: Why, then, did he call before seeing you, and before knowing you had even returned from Bristol?
“Witness (plainly confused): I cannot explain it.
“A Juryman: When you went back after hearing the cry and found your father dying, did you see anything suspicious?
“Witness: Nothing I could be certain of.
“The Coroner: What do you mean by that?

“Witness: When I rushed into the clearing, I was too distressed and agitated to think of anything but my father. Still, I vaguely remember something on the ground to my left as I ran forward. It seemed grey—a coat of some kind, or perhaps a plaid. After getting up from beside my father I looked for it, but it had disappeared.
“‘You mean it was gone before you left to fetch help?’
“‘Yes, it had disappeared.’
“‘You cannot identify what it was?’
“‘No. I only had the impression that something was there.’
“‘How far away from the body?’
“‘Roughly a dozen yards.’
“‘And how far was it from the wood's edge?’
“‘About that distance.’
“‘Then, if someone took it away, you were within a dozen yards when they did so?’
“‘Yes, but I had my back to it.’
“The witness's examination ended at this point.”

“I notice,” I said, reading down the column, “that the coroner was rather hard on young McCarthy in his concluding remarks. Quite reasonably, he stresses the inconsistency of the father's calling before seeing him, his refusal to explain their argument, and his odd report of the dying words. As the coroner says, all these points weigh heavily against the son.”

Holmes chuckled quietly and stretched out on the upholstered seat. “You and the coroner have worked hard to isolate the strongest arguments in his favour. Don't you see that you accuse him first of too little imagination, then of too much? Too little to invent a reason for the quarrel that would win the jury's sympathy; too much if he dreamed up something as _outré_ as a dying reference to a rat and a piece of cloth that disappeared. No, sir. I shall proceed on the assumption that the young man is telling the truth, and see where that leads. Now, here is my pocket edition of Petrarch. I shall say nothing further about the case until we reach the scene. We lunch at Swindon, which, I see, is twenty minutes away.”

After travelling through the lovely Stroud Valley and across the broad, shining Severn, we finally reached the pretty little country town of Ross at nearly four. A thin, ferret-like man with a sly, furtive look awaited us on the platform. His light-brown dustcoat and leather leggings were a concession to the countryside, but I easily recognised Scotland Yard's Lestrade. We drove with him to the Hereford Arms, where a room had been reserved.
“I have arranged for a carriage,” Lestrade said as we sat over our tea. “Knowing your energetic nature, I assumed you would not be satisfied until you had personally visited the scene of the crime.”
“Very thoughtful and flattering of you,” Holmes replied. “But it depends entirely on the barometric pressure.”
Lestrade looked taken aback. “I don't quite understand,” he said.

“What does the barometer say? Twenty-nine, I see. No wind, and a cloudless sky. I have a case of cigarettes that need smoking, and this sofa is far better than the usual country-hotel horror. I doubt I shall want the carriage this evening.”

Lestrade gave a laugh of indulgence. “No doubt the newspapers have already enabled you to form your conclusions. The case is perfectly plain, and closer examination only makes it plainer. Still, one cannot refuse a lady, especially one so determined. She has heard of you and insisted on your opinion, although I repeatedly explained that you could do nothing I hadn't done already. Why, bless my soul! Her carriage is outside now.”

Almost before he finished, one of the loveliest young women I have ever seen burst into the room. Her violet eyes shone, her lips were parted, and her cheeks flushed pink. Excitement and anxiety had swept away all her natural reserve.

“Oh, Mr. Sherlock Holmes!” she cried, looking between us before fixing on my companion with a woman's quick intuition. “I am so thankful you have come. I drove down just to tell you. I know James didn't do it. I know, and I want you to know it too before you begin. You must never doubt that. We have known one another since childhood. Nobody knows his faults better than I do, but he is too gentle to hurt a fly. To anyone who really knows him, the accusation is absurd.”
“I hope we can prove him innocent, Miss Turner,” Holmes said. “You may depend on me to do everything possible.”
“But you have read the evidence. Have you reached a conclusion? Can you see no weakness, no flaw in it? Don't you believe he is innocent?”
“I believe it is very likely that he is.”
“There!” she exclaimed, lifting her head and looking defiantly at Lestrade. “You hear him! He gives me hope.”
Lestrade shrugged his shoulders. “I am afraid my colleague has been rather quick in reaching his conclusions,” he replied.
“But he is right! Oh, I know he is! James didn't do it. As for the argument with his father, I am certain he wouldn't explain it to the coroner because it concerned me.”
“In what respect?” Holmes asked.

“This is not the moment to conceal anything. James and his father often disagreed over me. Mr. McCarthy badly wanted us to marry. James and I have always loved each other like brother and sister. But of course he is young and has seen very little of the world, and—and—well, naturally he did not want to take such a step yet. So they argued, and I am certain that was the reason for this argument too.”
“And your father?” Holmes asked. “Did he wish you to make that marriage?”
“No, he opposed it as well. Mr. McCarthy was the only one who wanted it.” A sudden blush crossed her fresh young face as Holmes gave her a sharp, enquiring glance.
“Thank you for telling me,” he said. “If I call tomorrow, might I see your father?”
“I am afraid his doctor would not permit it.”
“His doctor?”

“Yes. Haven't you heard? Poor Father has been in weak health for years, but this has completely broken him. He is in bed. Dr. Willows says he is a wreck, with his nervous system shattered. Mr. McCarthy was the only living person who had known Dad in the old days in Victoria.”
“Ah! Victoria! That is an important point.”
“Yes, when they were at the mines.”
“Of course—the gold mines, where I understand Mr. Turner acquired his fortune.”
“Yes, certainly.”
“Thank you, Miss Turner. What you have told me has been a real help.”
“Please let me know tomorrow if you learn anything. I expect you will visit James in prison. Oh, Mr. Holmes, if you do, please tell him I know he is innocent.”
“I shall tell him, Miss Turner.”

“I must return home now. Dad is terribly ill and misses me whenever I am away. Goodbye, and may God help you in your work.” She rushed out as impulsively as she had entered, and we heard her carriage rattle away along the street.
After a few silent minutes, Lestrade said with dignity, “I am ashamed of you, Holmes. Why encourage hopes that you must disappoint? I am not particularly tender-hearted, but I call that cruel.”
“I believe I can see a way to clear James McCarthy,” Holmes answered. “Do you have permission to visit him in prison?”
“Yes, but it covers only you and me.”
“Then I shall change my decision about going out. Can we still catch a train to Hereford and see him tonight?”
“There is plenty of time.”
“Then let us go. Watson, I am afraid this will leave you rather bored, but I should be back within a couple of hours.”

I accompanied them to the station, wandered through the small town, and finally returned to the hotel. There I lay on the sofa and tried to take an interest in a yellow-backed novel. Its feeble plot seemed insubstantial beside the deep mystery we were trying to penetrate. My thoughts kept straying from the fiction to the facts, until I threw the book across the room and devoted myself to the day's events. Suppose the unfortunate young man's account was entirely true. What dreadful, wholly unexpected calamity could have occurred between his leaving his father and his rushing back into the clearing at the sound of his cries? Something terrible and fatal had happened—but what? Could my medical knowledge extract anything from the injuries? I rang and asked for the county's weekly paper, which printed the inquest word for word. The surgeon testified that a heavy blow from a blunt weapon had shattered the rear third of the left parietal bone and the left half of the occipital bone. I located the area on my own head. Clearly the blow must have come from behind. That supported the accused to some extent: during the quarrel he had faced his father. Still, it proved little, since the older man might have turned away before being struck. Nevertheless, Holmes should perhaps have his attention drawn to it. Then there was that strange dying reference to a rat. What did it mean? It could not be delirium. A man dying from a sudden blow does not usually become delirious. More probably he was trying to explain his fate. But what could he mean? I struggled for a possible answer. And the grey cloth young McCarthy had seen: if that was true, the murderer must have dropped part of his clothing, presumably his overcoat, while escaping. He must then have been bold enough to return and retrieve it while the son knelt with his back turned, fewer than twelve paces away. What a web of mysteries and improbabilities! I could understand Lestrade's view. Yet I trusted Holmes's insight too much to abandon hope while each new fact seemed to confirm his belief in young McCarthy's innocence.
Holmes returned late that evening. He was alone; Lestrade had taken lodgings in the town.

“The barometer is still keeping very high,” he said, sitting down. “It is important that no rain fall before we examine the ground. Equally, such delicate work requires a man to be thoroughly fresh and alert. I didn't want to attempt it tired out by a long journey. I have seen young McCarthy.”
“What did he tell you that was useful?”
“Nothing.”
“Could he explain nothing at all?”

“Nothing. At one point I thought he might know the culprit and be protecting him or her. Now I am convinced he is as bewildered as the rest of us. He is not particularly quick-minded, though good-looking and, I believe, fundamentally decent.”
“I cannot admire his judgement,” I said, “if it is really true that he was unwilling to marry such a charming young woman as Miss Turner.”

“Ah, that conceals a rather painful story. He is passionately, desperately in love with her. But about two years ago, when he was little more than a boy and before he truly knew her—she had spent five years at boarding-school—the fool fell into the clutches of a Bristol barmaid and married her at a registry office. Nobody knows anything about it. Imagine his torment at being scolded for refusing to do what he would give his eyes to do, yet knows he cannot. That was the frenzy that made him fling up his hands when his father pressed him, during their final conversation, to propose to Miss Turner. He has no means of supporting himself, and his father, by all accounts a hard man, would have disowned him completely if he learned the truth. The three days in Bristol were spent with this barmaid wife. His father had no idea where he was. Remember that: it matters. Yet some good has come of the disaster. Learning from the newspapers that he was in grave trouble and might be hanged, the barmaid abandoned him altogether. She wrote that she already has a husband in the Bermuda Dockyard, so there is no real bond between them. I think that news has consoled young McCarthy for everything he has endured.”
“But if he is innocent, who committed the murder?”

“Ah! Who indeed? I particularly want you to consider two points. First, the murdered man had arranged to meet someone at the pool. It could not have been his son, who was away and whose return he could not predict. Second, the murdered man called ‘Cooee!’ before knowing the son was home. Those are the essential points on which this case turns. Now, if you please, let us discuss George Meredith, leaving all lesser matters until tomorrow.”
As Holmes had predicted, no rain fell, and morning came bright and cloudless. At nine Lestrade arrived with the carriage, and we set off for Hatherley Farm and Boscombe Pool.
“There is serious news today,” Lestrade remarked. “Mr. Turner at the Hall is reportedly so ill that they have almost given up hope of saving him.”
“An older man, I suppose?” Holmes asked.

“Around sixty. But living abroad damaged his constitution, and his health has been declining for some time. This affair has affected him badly. He was an old friend of McCarthy's and a great benefactor, too: I have learned that he let him occupy Hatherley Farm without paying rent.”
“Indeed! That is an interesting discovery,” said Holmes.
“Oh yes! He has assisted him in a hundred other ways. Everyone locally speaks of his kindness towards him.”

“Really! Doesn't it strike you as rather unusual that this McCarthy, apparently possessing little of his own and owing Turner so much, should nevertheless talk of marrying his son to Turner's daughter, presumably the heiress to the estate? And with such absolute confidence, as though all that was needed was a proposal and everything else would follow! It is stranger still because we know Turner himself opposed the idea. His daughter told us as much. Do you infer nothing from that?”
“Now we're off into deductions and inferences,” Lestrade said, winking at me. “Facts give me quite enough trouble, Holmes, without chasing after theories and fancies.”
“Quite right,” Holmes said meekly. “You do have considerable trouble with facts.”
“At any rate,” Lestrade replied with some heat, “I have grasped one fact you seem unable to get hold of.”
“And what would that be?”
“That the younger McCarthy killed the elder, and every theory to the contrary is pure moonshine.”
“Well, moonshine gives more light than fog,” Holmes said, laughing. “But unless I am very much mistaken, that is Hatherley Farm on our left.”

“Yes, that's the place.” It was a sprawling, comfortable-looking two-storey house, with a slate roof and large yellow patches of lichen on its grey walls. But the closed blinds and chimneys without smoke gave it a grief-stricken air, as if the horror still lay heavily over it. At the door, Holmes asked the maid to bring the boots her master wore when he died, and a pair belonging to the son, though not those he had worn that day. Holmes carefully measured them at seven or eight points. Then he asked to see the courtyard, and from there we followed the winding track towards the pool.

When he was hot on a trail like this one, Sherlock Holmes became a different man entirely. Anyone familiar only with Baker Street's quiet thinker and logician would scarcely have recognised him. His face grew flushed and dark, his brows drawing into two hard black lines. Beneath them his eyes glittered like steel. He bent his head, hunched his shoulders, and pressed his lips together; the veins in his long, muscular neck stood out like whipcord. His nostrils seemed to widen with an animal hunger for pursuit. He concentrated so completely that questions or remarks passed unheard, or at most drew a brief, impatient growl. Swift and silent, he followed the track across the meadows and through the woods towards Boscombe Pool. Like the whole district, the ground was damp and marshy. Numerous footprints marked both the path and the short grass along its sides. Sometimes he hurried; sometimes he stopped abruptly; once he made a small detour into a meadow. Lestrade and I followed. The detective looked indifferent and contemptuous. I watched with interest, convinced that every movement my friend made had a definite purpose.

Boscombe Pool is a little sheet of water edged with reeds, about fifty yards from bank to bank. It lies on the boundary between Hatherley Farm and the wealthy Mr. Turner's private park. Above the woods lining its farther side we could see projecting red pinnacles, marking the position of the landowner's house. On the Hatherley side the trees grew thickly. Between their edge and the lakeside reeds stretched a narrow belt of soaked grass, twenty paces across. Lestrade indicated the precise place where they had found the body. Indeed, the ground was so wet that I could plainly see the marks left by the stricken man's fall. Holmes's eager face and searching eyes showed me that he could read many other things in that trampled grass. He ran around like a dog trying to pick up a scent, then turned to Lestrade.
“Why did you go into the pool?” he asked.
“I searched with a rake, thinking we might find a weapon or some other clue. But how on earth did you—”

“Tut, tut! There is no time! The print of your left foot, turned inward, is everywhere. A mole could follow it, and there it disappears into the reeds. How easy this might have been if I had arrived before a herd of buffalo trampled and wallowed all over the ground! Here is where the lodge-keeper and his party came. They have obliterated every track for six or eight feet around the body. But here are three distinct sets made by the same feet.” He took out a lens and lay on his waterproof for a closer look, speaking more to himself than to us. “Young McCarthy's prints. He walked twice and ran fast once: the soles cut deeply, the heels hardly show. That agrees with his account. He ran when he saw his father on the ground. Here the father paced back and forth. And this mark? The gun-butt while the son stood listening. And this? Ha, ha! What have we here? Tiptoes! On tiptoe! Square toes, too—very unusual boots. They approach, retreat, then return. Of course: to retrieve the cloak. Now, where did they start?” He went back and forth, losing the trail and finding it again, until we were well inside the wood beneath a huge beech, the largest tree nearby. He worked around to its far side and dropped onto his face again with a small cry of satisfaction. He stayed there a long time, turning leaves and dry sticks, collecting what looked like dust in an envelope, and examining through his lens both the ground and the bark as high as he could reach. He also inspected and kept a jagged stone lying in the moss. Finally he followed a woodland path to the main road, where all trace disappeared.

“A case of considerable interest,” he remarked, his usual manner returning. “That grey house on the right must be the lodge. I shall go in for a word with Moran, and perhaps write a short note. Then we can drive back to lunch. Go on to the cab; I will join you shortly.”
About ten minutes later we regained the cab and drove back to Ross. Holmes still carried the stone he had found among the trees.
“This may be of interest, Lestrade,” he said, offering it. “It is the murder weapon.”
“I cannot see any marks.”
“There are no marks.”
“Then how can you tell?”
“Grass was growing beneath it, so it had been there only a few days. There was no sign of the place it had been taken from. It fits the injuries. And there is no trace of another weapon.”
“What about the murderer?”

“Tall, left-handed, with a limp in his right leg. He wears heavy-soled shooting boots and a grey cloak, smokes Indian cigars through a holder, and has a blunt penknife in his pocket. There are other indications, but those should give us enough to begin searching.”
Lestrade laughed. “I am afraid I still remain a sceptic,” he said. “Theories are all very well, but we must deal with a hard-headed British jury.”
“_Nous verrons_,” Holmes replied calmly. “Follow your method; I shall follow mine. I have business this afternoon and will probably take the evening train to London.”
“Leaving the case unresolved?”
“No, quite resolved.”
“But what about the mystery?”
“I have solved it.”
“Then who committed the crime?”
“The man I have just described.”
“But who is this man?”
“Surely establishing that cannot be difficult. There are not so many people in this district.”
Lestrade shrugged his shoulders. “I am a practical man. I cannot wander around the countryside hunting a left-handed gentleman with a bad leg. Scotland Yard would make me its laughing-stock.”
“Very well,” Holmes answered quietly. “You have had your opportunity. These are your lodgings. Goodbye; I shall send you a note before leaving.”
After dropping Lestrade at his lodgings, we went on to our hotel, where lunch was waiting. Holmes ate in silence, deep in thought, with the troubled look of a man facing a difficult choice.
“Watson,” he said after the table had been cleared, “sit here and let me hold forth for a moment. I am uncertain what to do, and would appreciate your advice. Light a cigar while I explain.”
“By all means, do.”

“Two features of young McCarthy's account immediately struck us both, though I took them in his favour and you against him. First, according to his account, his father called ‘Cooee!’ before seeing him. Second, there was that strange dying reference to a rat. He muttered several words, you understand, but that was the only one his son caught. We must start our investigation from those two points, assuming at the outset that the young man's story is entirely true.”
“What do you make of ‘Cooee!’, then?”

“Clearly it was not addressed to the son. As far as the father knew, his son was in Bristol. His being within earshot was pure chance. The cry was intended to attract the person McCarthy had arranged to meet. But ‘Cooee’ is a specifically Australian call, used between Australians. That gives us strong grounds to think the person expected at Boscombe Pool had spent time in Australia.”
“And what do you make of the rat?”
